docs.title: NG911 RFC Catalog
docs.text: This site organizes Internet standards that matter for Next Generation 9‑1‑1 (NG911). This collection is manually curated and non-exhaustive (if you think an RFC should be included, please file an Issue on Github. Each RFC included has summary information that was generated automatically by ChatGPT.

docs.title: Scope and categories
docs.text:
We focus on emergency‑calling and emergency‑routing standards, not generic SIP or other standards widely used for non-9-1-1 purposes. The (somewhat arbitrary) set of categories used throughout the site is as follows:

  • Representation — PIDF‑LO / civic / geodetic formats.
  • Acquisition — device ↔ LIS protocols (HELD, discovery).
  • Routing — LoST, service URNs, boundary maintenance.
  • Conveyance — SIP geolocation and additional data.
  • Framework — ECRIT framework / BCP documentation.
  • Privacy — GEOPRIV privacy architecture.

An RFC may belong to one or more categories.

docs.title: Representation (11)
docs.text:
• RFC 4119: A Presence-based GEOPRIV Location Object Format (PIDF-LO) (November 2005) Defines PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format–Location Object) extending PIDF (Presence Information Data Format) with geopriv location, usage-rules, baseline GML (Geography Markup Language) support, and S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) security
  • RFC 4589: Location Types Registry (July 2006) Creates an IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry and XML (Extensible Markup Language) schema for standardized location type tokens
  • RFC 5139: Revised Civic Location Format for PIDF-LO (February 2008) Revises the PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object) civic address schema with new elements, thoroughfare hierarchy, language tagging, and country/subdivision constraints
  • RFC 5491: PIDF-LO Usage Clarification, Considerations, and Recommendations (March 2009) Constrains PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object) usage and GML (Geography Markup Language) shapes for interoperable, routing-ready Internet location
  • RFC 5774: Civic Address Considerations for PIDF-LO and IANA Registry Definition (BCP 154) (March 2010) Guidelines and an IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry for national civic-address mappings in PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object), including a complete Austrian mapping
  • RFC 5808: Requirements for a Location-by-Reference Mechanism (May 2010) Requirements for LbyR (Location-by-Reference) using a location URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) to retrieve location via configuration and dereference with privacy and security controls
  • RFC 5870: A Uniform Resource Identifier for Geographic Locations ('geo' URI) (June 2010) Defines the 'geo' URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) for coordinates in a default CRS (Coordinate Reference System) of WGS-84 (World Geodetic System 1984), with optional uncertainty and parameter registry
  • RFC 5962: Dynamic Extensions to PIDF-LO (September 2010) Adds dynamic motion elements to PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object) for orientation, speed, and heading
  • RFC 6848: Specifying Civic Address Extensions in PIDF-LO (January 2013) Defines extensible civic-address elements for PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format–Location Object), adds DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) CAtype 40 for lossless translation, and requires namespace-qualified validation in LoST (Location-to-Service Translation)
  • RFC 7035: Relative Location Representation (October 2013) Extends PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format‑Location Object) to encode relative offsets from a reference, with XML (eXtensible Markup Language) and TLV (Type‑Length‑Value) formats plus optional map alignment metadata
  • RFC 7459: Representation of Uncertainty and Confidence in PIDF-LO (February 2015) Defines uncertainty and confidence for PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object), adds a confidence element with PDF (Probability Density Function) type, and algorithms for manipulating uncertain location

docs.title: Acquisition (13)
docs.text:

  • RFC 5223: Discovering LoST Servers Using DHCP (August 2008) Defines LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) server discovery via DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) by delivering a DNS (Domain Name System) domain name for subsequent resolution
  • RFC 5985: HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) (September 2010) Defines HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery), an L7 LCP (Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol) to fetch device location from a LIS (Location Information Server) by value (PIDF-LO: Presence Information Data Format-Location Object) or by reference (URI: Uniform Resource Identifier)
  • RFC 5986: Discovering the Local Location Information Server (LIS) (September 2010) Defines LIS (Location Information Server) discovery using DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) and U-NAPTR (URI-enabled Naming Authority Pointer) to obtain a HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) URI
  • RFC 6155: Use of Device Identity in HELD (March 2011) Extends HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) so a LIS (Location Information Server) can locate a target using explicit Device identifiers with privacy and authorization controls
  • RFC 6225: DHCP Options for Coordinate-Based Location Configuration Information (July 2011) Defines DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) v4/v6 options for coordinate-based LCI (Location Configuration Information) with uncertainty, resolution, altitude types, and datum handling (§2.1–§2.5)
  • RFC 6753: A Location Dereference Protocol Using HELD (October 2012) Defines dereferencing a location URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) via HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol)/TLS (Transport Layer Security) to obtain a PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object)
  • RFC 6915: Flow Identity Extension for HELD (April 2013) Extends HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) with a flow identity to identify a Device by the full 6‑tuple across NAT (Network Address Translation)
  • RFC 7105: Using Device-Provided Location-Related Measurements in LCPs (January 2014) Standardizes an XML container and schemas for device-provided measurements in LCP (Location Configuration Protocol) requests to a LIS (Location Information Server), with provenance, requests, and privacy/security controls
  • RFC 7199: Location Configuration Extensions for Policy Management (April 2014) Defines policy URIs and HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) extensions so LCP (Location Configuration Protocol) clients manage location-by-reference authorization via HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) GET/PUT/DELETE
  • RFC 7216: LIS Discovery Using IP Addresses and Reverse DNS (April 2014) Defines reverse DNS (Domain Name System)–based domain inputs from device IP addresses to discover an access-network LIS (Location Information Server) via DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service), including prefix-shortening in in-addr.arpa/ip6.arpa (§4–§4.3)
  • RFC 7840: A Routing Request Extension for HELD (May 2016) Extends HELD (HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery) to let a LIS (Location Information Server) return PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point) routing URIs with location, reducing dependency on LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) (§1, §4)

  • RFC 6281: LoST: An Extension for Finding Geographically Relevant Speakers of a Language (June 2011) Describes BTMM (Back to My Mac) using IPv6 ULA (Unique Local Address) identifiers, IPsec (Internet Protocol Security), and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) encapsulation to enable secure mobility across Network Address Translators
  • RFC 6442: Location Conveyance for the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) (December 2011) Adds SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) extensions to carry caller location by value or reference and to control location-based routing via Geolocation, Geolocation-Routing, and Geolocation-Error, plus a 424 error for bad location (§1, §4.1–§4.4)
  • RFC 6739: Synchronizing Service Boundaries and Elements Based on LoST (October 2012) Defines the LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) sync protocol to exchange authoritative mapping elements and service boundary data for correct PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point) selection
  • RFC 7163: URN for Country-Specific Emergency Services (March 2014) Updates RFC (Request for Comments) 5031 to allow sos service URN (Uniform Resource Name) registrations for country-specific emergency services (§3.2)

docs.title: RFC 4119: A Presence-based GEOPRIV Location Object Format
docs.text:
Proposed Standard November 2005

Representation

Abstract: This document describes an object format for carrying geographical information on the Internet. This location object extends the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), which was designed for communicating privacy-sensitive presence information and which has similar properties.

docs.title: Summary tagline
docs.text: Defines PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format–Location Object) extending PIDF (Presence Information Data Format) with geopriv location, usage-rules, baseline GML (Geography Markup Language) support, and S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) security

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Location-sharing applications lacked a standard, privacy-protective, and cryptographically secured way to convey user location and preferences; prior systems risked disclosure due to poor security and inability to express user policies (§1). Interoperability required an object that encapsulates existing formats with baseline support and minimal policy controls while fuller rulesets remained out of scope (§1, §2.2.2).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text: Extends PIDF (Presence Information Data Format) by defining geopriv with mandatory location-info (imported schemas), mandating baseline GML (Geography Markup Language) 3.0 feature.xsd support and optionally a civicAddress (civicLoc) schema (§2.2, §2.2.1, §2.2.5). Adds usage-rules with retransmission-allowed, retention-expiry, external-ruleset, and note-well to express privacy policies, plus optional method (enumerated via IANA: Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) and provided-by (IANA-registered XML namespaces) (§2.2.2–§2.2.4, §6.1–§6.2). Specifies carriage as application/pidf+xml, and requires end-to-end security using S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) with CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) EnvelopedData/SignedData and AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), with certificate/keying guidance (§3, §4).

docs.title: RFC 4589: Location Types Registry
docs.text:
Proposed Standard July 2006

Representation

Abstract: This document creates a registry for describing the types of places a human or end system might be found. The registry is then referenced by other protocols that need a common set of location terms as protocol constants. Examples of location terms defined in this document include aircraft, office, and train station.

docs.title: Summary tagline
docs.text: Creates an IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) registry and XML (Extensible Markup Language) schema for standardized location type tokens

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Protocols lacked a common, standardized set of place-type tokens to describe environments beyond raw civic/geospatial coordinates, limiting automated behavior and cross-language interoperability (§1). A controlled registration process was needed to extend terms without uncontrolled growth while ensuring conformance constraints (§1, §5.1).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text: Defines a registry of location type tokens (e.g., airport, public, restaurant, unknown) and an accompanying XML (Extensible Markup Language) schema/namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:location-type with elements typed mostly as empty and other as Note_t supporting xml:lang (§3, §4). Establishes IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) procedures: Expert Review for additions/updates and a requirement that tokens conform to XML Name character rules (§5.1). Registers a URN (Uniform Resource Name) sub-namespace and publishes the schema for reuse by other specifications (§5.2–§5.3). Clarifies that tokens can be used either as protocol constants or as XML elements referenced by other schemas (§4).

docs.title: RFC 4676: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) Option for Civic Addresses Configuration Information
docs.text:
Proposed Standard October 2006

Acquisition

Abstract: This document specifies a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCPv4 and DHCPv6) option containing the civic location of the client or the DHCP server. The Location Configuration Information (LCI) includes information about the country, administrative units such as states, provinces, and cities, as well as street addresses, postal community names, and building information. The option allows multiple renditions of the same address in different scripts and languages.

docs.title: Summary tagline
docs.text: Defines DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) options to convey structured civic address location with language/script variants to clients

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Emergency-capable endpoints need a standard way to obtain civic (street) location, not just coordinates, via DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) (§1). Civic formats vary by country and may require multiple languages/scripts, which DHCP cannot negotiate without a structured, multi-rendering option (§1, §3.4). Security/privacy constraints limit DHCP to server-to-client “sighting” delivery and caution against client updates (§1, §6).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text: Defines DHCPv4 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv4) option GEOCONF_CIVIC (code 99) and DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6) option OPTION_GEOCONF_CIVIC (code 37) carrying what, country code, and a sequence of civic elements (§3.1–§3.2). Specifies element encoding with CAtype/CAlength/CAvalue, a registry of CAtypes (initial list provided), and support for multiple renderings via language (CAtype 0) and script (CAtype 128), encoded in UTF-8 (Unicode Transformation Format-8) (§3.3–§3.4). Provides postal-address construction rules (e.g., PCN and P.O. Box override civic components), operational guidelines (v4/v6 data consistency, long options per RFC 3396), and security requirements (return only when requested; recommend authentication; avoid client-to-server location) (§1, §4, §6). Aligns civic components with NENA (National Emergency Number Association) terms and maps several elements to PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format-Location Object) to ease downstream location use (§3.4).

docs.title: Summary tagline
docs.text: Defines DHCPv4 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol v4) and DHCPv6 options to deliver civic/postal location (LCI: Location Configuration Information) with multi-language/script support for emergency and presence uses (§1, §3)

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: IP devices, especially IP telephony, need location to reach the correct emergency agency, but prior DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) mechanisms did not standardize conveying civic/postal addresses to clients (§1). Civic formats vary by country and there is no language/script negotiation in DHCP, necessitating a way to carry multiple renderings while addressing security/privacy concerns (§1, §3.4, §6).

docs.title: Contributions

docs.title: RFC 5491: GEOPRIV Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) Usage Clarification, Considerations, and Recommendations
docs.text:
Proposed Standard March 2009

Representation

Abstract: The Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO) specification provides a flexible and versatile means to represent location information. There are, however, circumstances that arise when information needs to be constrained in how it is represented. In these circumstances, the range of options that need to be implemented are reduced. There is growing interest in being able to use location information contained in a PIDF-LO for routing applications. To allow successful interoperability between applications, location information needs to be normative and more tightly constrained than is currently specified in RFC 4119 (PIDF-LO). This document makes recommendations on how to constrain, represent, and interpret locations in a PIDF-LO. It further recommends a subset of Geography Markup Language (GML) 3.1.1 that is mandatory to implement by applications involved in location-based routing.

Acquisition Privacy

Abstract: When a Location Information Server receives a request for location information (using the locationRequest message), described in the base HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) specification, it uses the source IP address of the arriving message as a pointer to the location determination process. Abstract: Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) maps service identifiers and location information to service contact URIs. If a LoST client wants to discover available services for a particular location, it will perform a query to the LoST server. docs.title: RFC 6280: An Architecture for Location and Location Privacy in Internet Applications
docs.text:
Best Current Practice July 2011

Privacy Framework

Abstract: Location-based services (such as navigation applications, emergency services, and management of equipment in the field) need geographic location information about Internet hosts, their users, and other related entities. These applications need to securely gather and transfer location information for location services, and at the same time protect the privacy of the individuals involved. This document describes an architecture for privacy-preserving location-based services in the Internet, focusing on authorization, security, and privacy requirements for the data formats and protocols used by these services. This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

docs.title: RFC 6444: Location Hiding: Problem Statement and Requirements
docs.text:
Informational January 2012

Privacy

Abstract: The emergency services architecture developed in the IETF Emergency Context Resolution with Internet Technology (ECRIT) working group describes an architecture where location information is provided by access networks to endpoints or Voice over IP (VoIP) service providers in order to determine the correct dial string and information to route the call to a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP). To determine the PSAP Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), the usage of the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol is envisioned.

This document provides a problem statement and lists requirements for situations where the Internet Access Provider (IAP) and/or the Internet Service Provider (ISP) are only willing to disclose limited or no location information. This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.

docs.title: Summary tagline
docs.text: Problem statement and requirements enabling location hiding by access providers while still supporting LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) routing and PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point) delivery

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: Many IAP (Internet Access Provider) and ISP (Internet Service Provider) operators are unwilling to disclose precise location to endpoints or VSPs (Voice Service Providers) for business, cost, or privacy reasons, yet emergency call routing and validation still require location (§1.2, §1.1). LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) requires Location-by-Value, so LbyR (Location-by-Reference) cannot be used for location-based routing or by independent VSP-operated LoST servers, complicating PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point) URI discovery/validation when location is hidden (§1.3).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text: Enumerates requirements (Req-1–Req-21) for solutions that let IAP (Internet Access Provider)/ISP (Internet Service Provider) operators withhold precise location from endpoints and VSPs (Voice Service Providers) while ensuring the PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point) receives precise location by value (§3). It requires that a VSP can validate emergency routing targets as bona fide LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) PSAP URIs, supports pre-call discovery of dial strings and PSAP/ESRP (Emergency Services Routing Proxy) URLs, and assumes no IAP–VSP business/trust relationship (§3). It constrains solutions to minimize UA changes, work without requiring SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) at access networks, interoperate with legacy devices and NATs, not burden non-hiding parties, and permit IP-to-PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) gateway routing (§3).

RFC 6739: Synchronizing Service Boundaries and Elements Based on the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Protocol

Experimental October 2012

Routing

Abstract: The Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol is an XML-based protocol for mapping service identifiers and geodetic or civic location information to service URIs and service boundaries. In particular, it can be used to determine the location-appropriate Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) for emergency services.

The element in the LoST protocol specification encapsulates information about service boundaries and circumscribes the region within which all locations map to the same service Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) or set of URIs for a given service.

This document defines an XML protocol to exchange these mappings between two nodes. This mechanism is designed for the exchange of authoritative elements between two entities. Exchanging cached elements, i.e., non-authoritative elements, is possible but not envisioned. Even though the element format is reused from the LoST specification, the mechanism in this document can be used without the LoST protocol. This document defines an Experimental Protocol for the Internet community.

docs.title: RFC 6772: Geolocation Policy: A Document Format for Expressing Privacy Preferences for Location Information
docs.text:
Proposed Standard January 2013

Privacy

Abstract: This document defines an authorization policy language for controlling access to location information. It extends the Common Policy authorization framework to provide location-specific access control. More specifically, this document defines condition elements specific to location information in order to restrict access to data based on the current location of the Target.

Furthermore, this document defines two algorithms for reducing the granularity of returned location information. The first algorithm is defined for usage with civic location information, whereas the other one applies to geodetic location information. Both algorithms come with limitations. There are circumstances where the amount of location obfuscation provided is less than what is desired. These algorithms might not be appropriate for all application domains.

docs.title: RFC 7090: Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) Callback
docs.text:
Proposed Standard April 2014

Framework Conveyance

Abstract: After an emergency call is completed (terminated either prematurely by the emergency caller or normally by the call taker), the call taker may feel the need for further communication. For example, the call may have been dropped by accident without the call taker having sufficient information about the current state of an accident victim. A call taker may trigger a callback to the emergency caller using the contact information provided with the initial emergency call. This callback could, under certain circumstances, be treated like any other call and, as a consequence, it may get blocked by authorization policies or may get forwarded to an answering machine.

The IETF emergency services architecture specification already offers a solution approach for allowing Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) callbacks to bypass authorization policies in order to reach the caller without unnecessary delays. Unfortunately, the specified mechanism only supports limited scenarios. This document discusses shortcomings of the current mechanisms and illustrates additional scenarios where better-than-normal call treatment behavior would be desirable. We describe a solution based on a new header field value for the SIP Priority header field, called "psap-callback", to mark PSAP callbacks.

It fails with routing asymmetry, multi-stage routing, call forwarding, and network-based Service URN resolution; PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) interworking is out of scope (§3.1–§3.4, §3.5).

Registers the new psap-callback value in the SIP Priority Header Field Values registry (§6).

Proposed Standard July 2016

Conveyance

Abstract: When an emergency call is sent to a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), the originating device, the access network provider to which the device is connected, and all service providers in the path of the call have information about the call, the caller, or the location, which is helpful for the PSAP to have in handling the emergency. This follows the tradition of prior emergency services standardization work where data can be conveyed by value within the call signaling (i.e., in the body of the SIP message) or by reference.

docs.text:
Proposed Standard May 2017

Conveyance

Abstract: This document describes how to use IP-based emergency services mechanisms to support the next generation of emergency calls placed by vehicles (automatically in the event of a crash or serious incident, or manually invoked by a vehicle occupant) and conveying vehicle, sensor, and location data related to the crash or incident. Such calls are often referred to as "Automatic Crash Notification" (ACN), or "Advanced Automatic Crash Notification" (AACN), even in the case of manual trigger. The "Advanced" qualifier refers to the ability to carry a richer set of data.

This document also registers a MIME media type and Emergency Call Data Type for the vehicle, sensor, and location data (often referred to as "crash data" even though there is not necessarily a crash) and an INFO package to enable carrying this and related data in SIP INFO requests. An external specification for the data format, contents, and structure is referenced in this document.

This document reuses the technical aspects of next-generation Pan- European eCall (a mandated and standardized system for emergency calls by in-vehicle systems (IVSs) within Europe and other regions). However, this document specifies use of a different set of vehicle (crash) data, specifically, the Vehicle Emergency Data Set (VEDS) rather than the eCall Minimum Set of Data (MSD). This document is an extension of the IETF eCall document, with the primary differences being that this document makes the MSD data set optional and VEDS mandatory, and it adds attribute values to the metadata/control object to permit greater functionality. This document registers a new INFO package (identical to that registered for eCall but with the addition of the VEDS MIME type). This document also describes legacy (circuit-switched) ACN systems and their migration to next-generation emergency calling, to provide background information and context.

Abstract: Use of the Internet for emergency calling is described in RFC 6443, 'Framework for Emergency Calling Using Internet Multimedia'. In some cases of emergency calls, the transmission of application data is all that is needed, and no interactive media channel is established: a situation referred to as 'non-interactive emergency calls', where, unlike most emergency calls, there is no two-way interactive media such as voice or video or text. docs.text:
Proposed Standard October 2020

Routing

Abstract: This document adds the 'LoST-Validation' service tag to the Straightforward-Naming Authority PoinTeR (S-NAPTR) Application Service Tag IANA registry. This tag can appear in a Naming Authority Pointer (NAPTR) Domain Name System (DNS) record to assist clients of the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Protocol in identifying LoST servers designated for location validation. This tag and the information about its use update RFC 5222, which enables the explicit discovery of a server that supports location validation.

docs.title: Summary tagline
docs.text: Registers the LoST-Validation S-NAPTR (Straightforward-Naming Authority PoinTeR) tag so LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) clients can discover DNS (Domain Name System) NAPTR (Naming Authority Pointer) records for servers designated for location validation

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) clients could not explicitly discover servers designated for validation because referrals return an AUS (Application Unique String), not a URL (Uniform Resource Locator), and servers may ignore validation requests (§2). DNS naming conventions to separate mapping and validation are fragile, and NENA i3 (National Emergency Number Association IP-based architecture) requires separable ECRF (Emergency Call Routing Function) and LVF (Location Validation Function), increasing the need for distinct discovery (§2). This reduces the chance that validation queries hit servers not performing validation, an issue noted since RFC 5582 (§2).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text: Registers the LoST-Validation tag in the S-NAPTR registry, complementing LoST, and updates discovery so clients can explicitly locate validation-designated servers (§3, §6.1, §1). Specifies client behavior: resolve via U-NAPTR (URI-Enabled NAPTR) within DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery Service) using LoST-Validation, use HTTP/HTTPS URLs, and fall back to LoST if LoST-Validation does not yield a usable server (§3). Describes backward compatibility, including the locationValidationUnavailable warning and optional <redirect> with an AUS to alternate servers (§4).

Abstract: This document changes the policy of the "Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Location Profiles" IANA registry established by RFC 5222 from Standards Action to Specification Required. This allows standards development organizations (SDOs) other than the IETF to add new values.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text: The LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) protocol uses location profiles, but the LoST Location Profiles registry required a Standards Track RFC (Request for Comments) for any new values (§1). This prevented SDOs (Standards Development Organizations) such as NENA (National Emergency Number Association) from adding needed profiles, limiting non-IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) extensions (§1).

docs.title: Contributions
docs.text: Changes the registry policy for the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) Location Profiles from Standards Action to Specification Required, enabling SDOs (Standards Development Organizations) beyond the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) to register new values (§2, §4). Designates an Expert Reviewer per RFC (Request for Comments) 8126 and specifies review checks: the value is specified by an appropriate SDO, has a clear need with no existing profile meeting it, and is unambiguous and interoperable (§4). Adds this document as a reference for the registry (§4).
